summary: Supply the income in 2019 and the income in 2018 and the Second stimulus check calculator solves for you will receive. Think of it as a shortcut for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Second stimulus check calculator work?
sections.html:
The Second stimulus check calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports you will receive in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (have you filed 2019 taxes? and the filing status); then you type in how many kids?, the income in 2019 (AGI) and the income in 2018 (AGI).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as yes and no. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as single, married and head of household. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Second stimulus check calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

You will receive=(filing status, how many kids?, income in 2019 (AGI))
You will receive=(filing status, how many kids?, income in 2018 (AGI))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Second stimulus check calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the income in 2019 and the income in 2018 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Second stimulus check calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The 2 drop-downs on this page offer a fixed list of cases. A value that is not on the list cannot be entered, and the nearest option is not always a good substitute.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — have you filed 2019 taxes? for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Second stimulus check calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns you will receive, derived from the income in 2019 and the income in 2018. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Second stimulus check calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the income in 2019 and the income in 2018, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Second stimulus check calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
